text: You have never really seen the ocean. You've seen its roof.
Everything you picture — every beach, every reef, every shark — is in the top two hundred metres. The bottom is nearly eleven kilometres down.
Twelve levels. We're going down all of them, one at a time, with real footage from as deep as cameras can go. And we are not coming back up.
Level one is the only one you've ever been to.
Here's the number that puts this whole video in perspective. Forty metres.
That's the limit for recreational scuba diving — as deep as a trained holiday diver is ever meant to go.
Forty metres. The sea floor is, on average, ninety times deeper than that.
This is the sunlight zone, the top two hundred metres, and it's the only part of the sea that behaves the way you expect.
Sunlight means plants — mostly ones too small to see, single-celled algae called phytoplankton.
And these specks do something enormous. About half of the oxygen produced on Earth is produced in the sea — most of it by drifting life you would need a microscope to see.
But the ocean is already taking things away. The first to go is colour.
Water swallows red light first, and by a hundred metres, red is completely gone. A bright red fish down here simply looks black.
Hold on to that. Four levels from now, it turns into a superpower.
Level one of twelve. Let's find the line where the plants stop.
Two hundred metres. Look up, and there's still a soft blue glow above you. But it's no longer enough.
Below this line there isn't enough light for photosynthesis — so from about here to the bottom of the sea, it's animals and microbes only.
Welcome to the twilight zone. It runs from here down to a thousand metres: just enough light for animals to see by, far too little for a plant to live on.
And that creates a strange problem. There is nowhere to hide.
No rocks, no weeds, no sea floor — only open water, and a faint light above that turns your body into a silhouette for anything looking up from below.
So the animals here cheat. Hatchetfish and lanternfish carry rows of tiny lamps along their bellies, and they tune the glow to match the light coming down from the surface.
From underneath, the shadow simply… disappears.
It's called counter-illumination. The first lights in the deep aren't for seeing. They're for not being seen.
Two levels down. The next one is the deepest a human being has ever gone on their own.
Three hundred and thirty-two metres. This is as deep as any human has ever gone with scuba tanks.
In 2014, an Egyptian diver named Ahmed Gabr descended here, in the Red Sea, to set the world record.
Getting down took him about fifteen minutes.
Getting back up took more than thirteen and a half hours.
That's not a mistake — and the reason is the whole problem with the deep.
At this pressure, the nitrogen in every breath he takes dissolves into his blood and tissues. The deeper he goes, the more of it goes in.
Come up quickly, and that nitrogen comes back out of solution inside him — as bubbles. In the joints. In the spine. In the brain.
Divers call it the bends. It can cripple you, and it can be fatal.
So the only way home is to stop. And wait. And let his body breathe the nitrogen back out, a little at a time, stop after stop, hanging on a line in the blue for thirteen and a half hours.
He trained four years for this and had a team of thirty people. It is a record for professionals, not something to try.
The ocean lets you down for free. It charges you to come back.
And here's the thing to understand about the ocean. For a human body with tanks, this is more or less the end of the road.
For the ocean, we're not even a tenth of the way to the average sea floor.
And just below him is something that fooled an entire navy.
Around five hundred metres, the navy found a second sea floor. One that should not have been there.

During the Second World War, sonar operators hunting submarines kept getting the same impossible reading: solid ground, a few hundred metres down, in places where the charts said the water was kilometres deep.
And this floor moved. Every evening it rose toward the surface. Every dawn, it sank back down.
They checked the equipment. They suspected the enemy was jamming them. Neither explanation held.
In 1945 a scientist named Martin Johnson worked out what it was. It wasn't rock. It was alive.
Billions upon billions of small animals — tiny fish, shrimp, jellies, plankton — spend their days down here in the gloom, where hunters can't see them.
At sunset they swim up to the food-rich surface to feed under cover of night. Before sunrise, they all go back down.
NOAA calls it the greatest migration on Earth. It happens every day, in every ocean… and the entire thing takes place in the dark.
And the scale of it is difficult to hold in your head. Current estimates put it at something like ten billion tonnes of animals, rising and sinking, every single day.
It isn't only a commute, either. Every one of those animals feeds up at the surface and then carries that food — that carbon — back down with it into the deep, where a great deal of it stays.
The largest daily movement of life on this planet is also one of its great carbon pumps.
And we only noticed it because it got in the way of a war.
Four levels down, eight to go. And this is where the light finally runs out completely.
One thousand metres. This is about as deep as sunlight can be detected at all. Below here, it is night — permanently.
And yet it isn't dark.

When scientists in California counted every animal in seventeen years of deep-sea robot footage — more than three hundred and fifty thousand of them — they found that three out of four can make their own light.
Down here, glowing isn't unusual. Glowing is normal: lures to attract a meal, flashes to find a partner, bursts of light to startle a hunter and slip away.
Now look at the colour of it. Nearly all of that light is blue — over and over, the same narrow band of blue.
That isn't decoration. Blue is the wavelength that travels furthest through seawater, so a blue flash carries further down here than any other colour could.
The sea filtered out red at a hundred metres. Life answered in blue.
Which brings us back to that red fish. No red light reaches this world, so an animal that is red has nothing to reflect — it is, effectively, invisible.
That's why so many deep-sea animals are red. Down here, red is the best camouflage in the ocean.
The water now is around four degrees Celsius, and it will stay about that cold all the way down.
Five levels down, seven to go. And the next one breaks a rule everybody thought was unbreakable.
Two and a half kilometres. In February 1977, a three-person submersible called Alvin was exploring a volcanic crack in the sea floor near the Galápagos Islands, looking for hot springs.
It found them. It also found something nobody had predicted: a garden.
Clams a foot long. Tube worms as tall as a person, crowded around vents where the water comes out of the rock at more than seven hundred degrees Fahrenheit — about three hundred and seventy Celsius.
No sunlight has ever touched this place. So what is everything eating?
The answer rewrote the textbooks. Microbes here live on chemicals dissolved in the vent water, and everything else lives on the microbes.
It was the first ecosystem ever found on Earth that doesn't run on sunlight. It runs on the planet itself.
And the tube worms are stranger than they look. A grown one has no mouth. No stomach. No gut at all.
What it has instead is an organ stuffed with bacteria — and in a big worm, that bacterial cargo can be something like a third to a half of its body weight.

The worm's whole job is to be a delivery system. That red plume at the top pulls in oxygen and hydrogen sulfide — the rotten-egg chemical that is poisonous to you and me — and its blood carries both down to the bacteria inside.
They turn the poison into food.
The worm never eats. Not once in its life. It simply breathes, and is fed from within.
More than five hundred of these vent fields have been found since — and they're one reason scientists take dark oceans on other worlds so seriously.
Six down. Now the record that beats every human being who has ever lived.
Sperm whales hunt giant squid more than two kilometres down. But they don't hold the record.
That belongs to a shy, medium-sized whale most people have never heard of: Cuvier's beaked whale.
In a study off California, scientists tracked one to two thousand nine hundred and ninety-two metres. Nearly three kilometres. Another dive lasted a hundred and thirty-seven minutes.
More than two hours. On one breath. In the cold and the dark, under about three hundred times the pressure you're feeling right now.
How is that even possible? By giving up on breathing altogether.
On the way down, the whale's ribcage folds and its lungs deliberately collapse. That sounds like a catastrophe.
It's a defence: with the lungs shut down, nitrogen can't cross into the blood — so the whale simply never gets the problem that cost our record-breaking diver thirteen and a half hours.
The oxygen it runs on isn't in its lungs at all. It's stored in its blood and packed into its muscle, which carries roughly ten times more of the oxygen-holding protein than ours does.
Its heart rate drops. Blood pulls back from the edges of the body toward the heart and brain.
For two hours, it stops being a mammal that breathes, and becomes something much closer to a submarine.
Remember Level 3? The best-prepared human diver in history turned around at three hundred and thirty-two metres. This whale goes nine times deeper — for lunch.
Seven levels down. And just past the limit of the deepest-diving mammal on Earth, something famous is lying in the dark.
Three thousand eight hundred metres. On the sea floor, about three hundred and seventy miles off Newfoundland, lies the most famous shipwreck in the world.
Titanic sank in 1912. Nobody saw her again until the first of September, 1985 — seventy-three years later — in part because it took that long to build machines that could search this deep.
But here's the part that should change how you picture the planet. We have just passed three thousand six hundred and eighty-two metres.
That is the average depth of the ocean.
Average.
Everything so far — the last plant, the record dive, the great migration, the whales — all of it happened above the average sea floor.
Picture the ocean floor anywhere in the world, and the honest picture is this: Titanic, in the dark, with nothing around it.
And she is being eaten.
Those rust-coloured icicles hanging off her railings have a name — rusticles — and they are alive. They are colonies of bacteria and fungi, consuming the iron of the ship itself.
One of the species found in them was new to science, and was named after the wreck it was eating: Halomonas titanicae.
Researchers disagree about the timetable. They don't disagree about the direction.
Titanic is being digested — and everything we ever learn about the most famous object in the deep sea, we have to learn inside a window that is closing.
And we are still only a third of the way down.
Below four thousand metres the ocean has an honest name: the abyss. The water is a few degrees above freezing. The pressure is four to six hundred times the surface.
And the landscape is mostly wide, quiet plains of soft mud.
No food is made down here. None. So the abyss lives on leftovers.
Far above, things die, and crumbs drift downward — scraps of plankton, dust, waste. Scientists call it marine snow, and some flakes fall for weeks before they land.
A whole world of animals — sea cucumbers, brittle stars, pale fish — spends its entire life waiting for the snow.
And don't picture somewhere small. NOAA puts the abyssal plains at around seventy per cent of the ocean floor.
Which means this — flat, freezing, permanently dark mud — is the largest habitat on Earth.
Not the rainforest. Not the grasslands. This.
The default condition of our planet's surface is a dark plain under four kilometres of water, waiting for crumbs to fall.
Nine levels down. And here the ordinary sea floor simply ends.
Six thousand metres is where the ordinary sea floor runs out. To go deeper, you need a trench.
This is the hadal zone — named after Hades, the Greek underworld — and it exists only inside these long, narrow scars in the ocean floor.
And trenches aren't holes. They're seams.
Out here the Pacific plate — old, cold and heavy — is bending downward and sliding underneath its neighbour, back into the mantle. The trench is the crease that makes.
The deepest place on Earth is, quite literally, where the sea floor goes to be recycled.

You might expect nothing here. Instead, in 2019, a camera lowered into the Java Trench filmed a dumbo octopus — a small octopus that swims by flapping two ear-like fins — calmly going about its day at six thousand nine hundred and fifty-seven metres.
It's the deepest octopus ever recorded.
Two levels left. And the next one is a line that nothing with a backbone has ever crossed.
Eight thousand three hundred and thirty-six metres. In 2022, in a trench south of Japan, scientists filmed a small, pale snailfish. It is the deepest fish anyone has ever seen.
And it may be close to the deepest a fish can be.
Deep-sea fish hold themselves together with a molecule called TMAO.
Think of it as chemical scaffolding: it keeps proteins in shape when pressure tries to fold them, and the deeper a fish lives, the more of it it packs into its cells.
But scaffolding has a ceiling. At somewhere around eight thousand two hundred metres, a fish would need so much TMAO that the rest of its body chemistry stops working.
The wall isn't the pressure itself. The wall is that a fish, built the way fish are built, runs out of the chemistry to answer it.
Below that line, as far as anyone has ever found: no fish. Anywhere.
There are still more than two and a half kilometres to go.
Ten thousand nine hundred and thirty-five metres. Challenger Deep, in the Mariana Trench, south-west of Guam.
If you stood Mount Everest in here, its summit would still be about two kilometres under water.
The pressure is more than a thousand times the surface — roughly eight tons on every square inch.
Humans first came here on the twenty-third of January, 1960. Two men, Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh, inside a steel sphere, sinking for nearly five hours.
On the way down, an outer window cracked with a bang that shook the whole craft. They kept going. They spent twenty minutes on the bottom.
Then, for fifty-two years, nobody went back at all. James Cameron went down alone in 2012. And since 2019, a single submarine has carried the great majority of everyone who has ever made the trip.
Today, more than twenty people have stood — or rather, sat — at the deepest place on Earth. That is more people than have ever walked on the Moon.
And even here, there is life. Tiny shrimp-like animals called amphipods live in Challenger Deep, feeding on whatever sinks this far — including, of all things, wood.
Twelve levels. A sunlit skin we all know. A twilight of animals that hide by glowing. A nightly migration bigger than anything on land. Gardens that never needed the Sun.
And eleven kilometres down, in permanent darkness, small animals getting on with their lives.
And here's the part that keeps oceanographers up at night. Of that entire eleven-kilometre stack, only about twenty-nine per cent of the sea floor has ever been properly mapped.
So — that roof we started on?
Most of what's under it is still a blank space on the map.
Next: the animals that actually live down here — every type of deep-sea creature, and the trick each one uses to survive.
